topics.title: Algebra 2: Quadratic Expressions
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: recognise equivalent quadratic expressions. (k u s)
solve quadratic equations where the quadratic expression can be factorised. (k s)

body.text: Namubiru plans a rectangular vegetable garden in Masaka. It is x + 3 metres long and x + 2 metres wide, so its area is (x + 3)(x + 2) square metres. Multiplying out the brackets gives x² + 5x + 6. An expression like this, where the highest power of x is 2, is called a quadratic expression.

To expand means to multiply out the brackets. For one bracket, multiply each term inside by the term outside: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. For two brackets, multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second. Then collect like terms, which have the same letter and power.
A rectangle helps. Split a rectangle of length x + 3 and width x + 2 into four parts. The parts have areas x², 3x, 2x and 6. Together they make x² + 5x + 6.

body.speech: x plus a, times x plus b, equals x squared plus a plus b times x, plus a b

body.text: Two expressions are equivalent when they give the same value for every value of x. (x + 3)(x + 5) and x² + 8x + 15 are equivalent: one is in brackets and one is expanded. Substituting a number is a quick check. When x = 2, (2 + 3)(2 + 5) = 35, and 4 + 16 + 15 = 35.
Perfect squares and the difference of two squares
A perfect square is an expression that is a bracket multiplied by itself. Its last term is a square number, and its middle term is twice the product of x and that square root.

body.speech: x plus a, all squared, equals x squared plus 2 a x plus a squared
x squared minus a squared equals x plus a, times x minus a

body.title: Spot perfect squares and use the difference of two squares
steps: x² + 6x + 9: 9 = 3² and 6x = 2 × 3 × x. So it is the perfect square (x + 3)².
x² + 6x + 8: 8 is not a square number, so this is not a perfect square.
Evaluate 101² − 99² without squaring: (101 + 99)(101 − 99) = 200 × 2 = 400.

body.text: Factorising is the reverse of expanding. We write the expression as a product of brackets. Always look first for a common factor: 3x² + 6x = 3x(x + 2).
For x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to give c and add to give b. Those two numbers go into the brackets.

body.title: Factorise three quadratic expressions
steps: x² + 7x + 12: we need two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7. These are 3 and 4. So x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4).
x² − 2x − 15: we need a product of −15 and a sum of −2. These are −5 and 3. So x² − 2x − 15 = (x − 5)(x + 3).
Check by expanding: (x − 5)(x + 3) = x² + 3x − 5x − 15 = x² − 2x − 15.
2x² + 7x + 3: multiply 2 by 3 to get 6. Find two numbers with product 6 and sum 7: 6 and 1.
Split the middle term: 2x² + 6x + x + 3 = 2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3) = (2x + 1)(x + 3).

body.text: If two numbers multiply to give zero, at least one of them must be zero. So when (x − 3)(x − 7) = 0, either x − 3 = 0 or x − 7 = 0. A quadratic equation usually has two solutions.

body.title: The sum is 10 and the product is 21
steps: The sum of two numbers is 10 and their product is 21. Let one number be x. The other is 10 − x.
Product: x(10 − x) = 21, so 10x − x² = 21.
Rearrange so one side is zero: x² − 10x + 21 = 0.
Factorise: (x − 3)(x − 7) = 0.
So x = 3 or x = 7. The two numbers are 3 and 7. Check: 3 + 7 = 10 and 3 × 7 = 21.

body.title: Find the size of a garden
steps: A rectangular garden in Mbarara is 3 m longer than it is wide. Its area is 40 m². Let the width be x metres.
Two numbers with product −40 and sum 3 are 8 and −5. So (x + 8)(x − 5) = 0.
x = −8 or x = 5. A width cannot be negative, so x = 5.
The garden is 5 m wide and 8 m long. Check: 5 × 8 = 40 m².

body.title: Build rectangles from tiles
body.text: Cut tiles from an old cardboard box. Make large squares of side x, long strips of length x and width 1, and small squares of side 1. To show x² + 5x + 6, take one large square, five strips and six small squares. Arrange all the tiles into one rectangle. Measure its two sides in terms of x. Try again with x² + 4x + 4. What is special about the shape this time?
x² − 4 can be factorised as (x + 2)(x − 2), but x² + 4 cannot be factorised using whole numbers. What makes the difference between the two?

To expand, multiply every term in one bracket by every term in the other. To factorise x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. Learn (x + a)² = x² + 2ax + a² and x² − a² = (x + a)(x − a). To solve a quadratic equation, make one side zero, factorise, then set each bracket equal to zero.
